name: Omaha
coverage: The City of Omaha, divided into ZIP Code Tabulation Areas clipped to the city limits, because the city publishes no clean neighborhood partition in open data. ZIP areas are larger than neighborhoods and are named by number, with mapped neighborhood names listed where OpenStreetMap has them. Not ranked (fewer than 500 residents): ZIP 68007, ZIP 68010, ZIP 68142.

sources.name: City limits: Omaha city (TIGERweb incorporated places)
sources.notes: Everything is counted inside the legal city limits only: residents, amenities and incidents outside them are left out.

sources.name: 2020 ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (TIGERweb)
sources.notes: ZCTAs approximate USPS ZIP code delivery areas. Each is clipped to the city limits.

sources.name: 2020 Census blocks: population, housing units and internal points (TIGERweb)
sources.notes: Each block is placed in the neighborhood containing its internal point. Tract-level ACS figures are then split between neighborhoods by the share of the tract’s 2020 residents (or housing units, for renter figures) in each.

sources.name: American Community Survey tables B01003 (population), B25031 (median gross rent by bedrooms), B25042 (tenure by bedrooms)
sources.notes: Gross rent is contract rent plus estimated utilities and fuels paid by the renter. It covers all renters, including long-term and subsidized tenants, so it runs below current asking rents.

sources.name: Small Area Fair Market Rents, FY2026
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
sources.observationPeriod: FY2026 (effective October 1, 2025), from recent-mover rents trended forward
sources.notes: The 40th percentile gross rent paid by recent movers, by ZIP code. Joined to tracts with the Census 2020 ZCTA–tract relationship file, taking the ZCTA covering most of each tract. A ZIP-level figure, not a neighborhood asking rent.

sources.name: 2020 ZCTA to Census Tract Relationship File
LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES 8), workplace area characteristics, 2023
sources.publisher: U.S. Census Bureau, Center for Economic Studies
sources.notes: Used only to flag areas where jobs outnumber residents, where per-resident incident rates need care.

sources.name: OpenStreetMap amenities and stations (via Overpass API)
sources.notes: Counts of mapped features: OSM shop=supermarket or shop=greengrocer; OSM leisure=park; OSM amenity=restaurant or amenity=cafe; OSM amenity=bar, pub or nightclub; OSM railway=station or halt, and light-rail/subway stops; OSM highway=bus_stop; OSM leisure=dog_park. Completeness depends on volunteer mapping and varies by area.

definitions.violent: Homicide, robbery and all assaults. Omaha publishes NIBRS offense groups only, so aggravated and simple assault cannot be separated, and sex offenses are not published.
definitions.property: Burglary, larceny/theft, motor vehicle theft and arson (NIBRS offense groups).
definitions.vehicle: Motor vehicle theft only: theft from vehicles is not separated from other larceny.

incidentMethod.dedupe: Counted as distinct report numbers per measure.
notes: Violent counts here include simple assaults, so they run higher than in cities that count aggravated assault only. Compare Omaha neighborhoods with each other, not with other cities.
Reported offenses, not calls for service or arrests.

Rates are reported incidents per 1,000 residents per year, using 2020–2024 ACS 5-year estimates population allocated to neighborhoods by 2020 block populations. They are not shown for areas with fewer than 2,000 residents.
